Bemoan
be-MOHN
verb
From the Saxon be, an intensive prefix, and maenan, to moan or lament. To moan over a person — the preposition is the point, for bemoaning is grief directed toward another, not merely felt within oneself.

Biblical Definition

To bemoan is to lament for someone, and Scripture treats the presence or absence of such lament as a measure of a people’s standing. Jeremiah’s question over the ruined city is unbearable precisely because it expects the answer none: “who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest?” (Jer 15:5). To be unmourned is the last stage of desolation; Nineveh receives the same sentence — “who will bemoan her?” (Nah 3:7). More solemn still is Jer 16:5, where the LORD forbids the prophet to lament at all: Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them. When God withdraws permission to grieve, judgment has passed beyond the reach of tears. And Jeremiah teaches the church how to aim its sorrow rightly: “Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away” (Jer 22:10). The dead are past our help; the man carried into exile who shall return no more is the fitter object of grief. That principle governs Christian mourning still. We sorrow for the departed saint, but not as others which have no hope; the heavier weeping belongs to those going away from God while still alive.

Webster 1828 Definition

To lament or bewail on another’s behalf; to express grief for a person or place. To be unbemoaned is, in the prophets, the mark of a completed judgment.

BEMOAN, v.t. To lament; to bewail; to express sorrow for.

From the Saxon be and maenan, to moan, to complain.

Distinguished from mere moaning by its object: one bemoans another, not oneself.

In the prophets, to be left unbemoaned is the extremity of desolation (Jer 15:5; Nah 3:7).

The prohibition of bemoaning is itself a judgment (Jer 16:5).

Key Scripture

Jer 15:5 — "For who shall have pity upon thee, O Jerusalem? or who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest?"

Jer 16:5 — "For thus saith the LORD, Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people, saith the LORD, even lovingkindness and mercies."

Jer 22:10 — "Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country."

Nah 3:7 — "And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?"

Modern Corruption

Modern religion has largely lost public lament, treating sustained grief as a problem to be resolved rather than a duty owed — while Scripture makes the absence of mourners a sign of judgment, not of health.

expand to see more

The corruption is the abolition of lament. Contemporary church life has little room for sorrow that does not resolve within the hour; grief is handled as a stage to be moved through, and the mourner is quietly urged toward recovery so that the congregation may return to its accustomed brightness. Scripture is far more spacious. A third of the Psalter laments, an entire book is called Lamentations, and the prophets bemoan cities aloud and at length. Jeremiah did not weep because he lacked faith; he wept because he saw clearly. To lose the vocabulary of lament is not to become more joyful but to become shallower, and it leaves the genuinely bereaved with no language the church will accept.

Recover the plain sense: bemoaning is an act of love aimed outward, and Jer 22:10 tells us where to aim it hardest. We instinctively pour our grief upon the dead, where it can do nothing, and withhold it from the living who are walking away. Reverse that. Weep sore for the son who goeth away, for the friend hardening under the word, for the nation being carried off — those are the mourners’ proper business. And take Jer 16:5 as a warning: there is a point at which God forbids the tears, and it is a mercy to be still permitted to weep.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon be + maenan, to moan over — grief directed toward another, whose absence marks a finished judgment.

expand to see more

Bemoan — Saxon intensive be + maenan, to moan, lament.

The prefix carries the sense over or for: to moan on another’s account.

Jer 15:5 and Nah 3:7: to be unbemoaned is the last stage of ruin.

Jer 16:5: God may forbid lament, and the prohibition is itself judgment.

Jer 22:10 orders the priority — weep more for the exile than for the dead.

Usage

"Jer 22:10 redirects grief from the dead, past help, to the living going away."

"To be left with no one to bemoan you is the prophets’ picture of total desolation."

"Jer 16:5 shows that permission to mourn is itself a mercy."
